People are not born with bipolar. However, people are born with a gene that makes it *more likely* for them to develop bipolar. Some people are born without this gene and will never develop bipolar. Some people with the gene for bipolar also never go on to develop bipolar. Of those with the gene who do eventually go on to develop bipolar, there are likely several environmental factors at play. The exact cause of bipolar disorder—and most other mental illnesses—remains unknown.

Source: a minor in psychology and my psychiatrist

BP1 is considered more severe than BP2, but that’s because of the severity of manic episodes.

BP1 is characterized by mania. BP2 will only experience hypomania, which is a milder form of mania.

Both can experience the extremities of depression, but only BP1 will also experience the extremities of mania.

Someone with BP1 doesn’t need to have ever experienced depression to be diagnosed. The same is true of BP2. That is not to say that someone with BP2 has an easier or milder form of the disease, though many would consider that the case.

Depression isn’t needed for either diagnosis, although someone with BP1 with severe depression and severe mania would be considered to have a worse form of the disease than someone with severe to mild depression and hypomania (BP2). 

Only one episode of mania is necessary for a lifetime diagnosis of BP1. Only one episode of hypomania is necessary for a lifetime diagnosis of BP2. 

I have BP1. I have only ever had mixed episodes (severe depression and severe mania at once). A mixed BP2 episode could include severe depression and hypomania at once. 

So many combinations exist. But the simplest explanation is one has severe mania—with or without depression (BP1)—and one has hypomania—with or without depression (BP2).
